## Chapter 13

Minister Adams’s success in stopping the rebel rams fixed his position once for all in English society. From that moment he could afford to drop the character of diplomatist and assume what, for an American Minister in London, was an exclusive advantage—the character of a kind of American Peer of the Realm. The British never did things by halves. Once they recognized a man’s right to social privileges, they accepted him as one of themselves. Even the Times conceded it.

This Anglo-American form of diplomacy was chiefly undiplomatic, and had the peculiar effect of teaching a habit of diplomacy useless or mischievous everywhere but in London. Private secretary in the morning, son in the afternoon, young man about town in the evening—the only character Henry Adams never bore was that of diplomatist, except when he wanted a card to some great function. His diplomatic education was at an end; he seldom met a diplomat, and never had business with one. He drifted inevitably into society, and, do what he might, his next education must be one of English social life. Tossed between successive dilemmas, he reached his twenty-sixth birthday without the power of earning five dollars in any occupation.

He had failed to acquire any useful education; he should at least have acquired social experience. Curiously enough, he failed here also. He happened on a social still-stand. The Prince Consort was dead; the Queen had retired; the Prince of Wales was still a boy. In its best days Victorian society had never been “smart.” Style lingered in the background with the powdered footman, but, speaking socially, the Queen had no style save what she inherited. Balmoral was a startling revelation of royal taste. One’s eyes might be dazzled by jewels, but they were heirlooms; if any lady appeared well dressed, she was either a foreigner or “fast.” Fashion was not fashionable in London until the Americans and the Jews were let loose. The style of London toilette in 1864 was grotesque.

His own want of experience prevented his asking introductions to the ladies who ruled society; his want of friends prevented his knowing who these ladies were; and he had every reason to expect snubbing if he put himself in evidence. He was son and private secretary too; he could not be as thick-skinned as an Englishman. The barrier was real, and sometimes frankly avowed.

“I don’t think I care for foreigners!”

He heard Lady Margaret Beaumont say it to herself, in her rich voice, looking into her tea-cup. Horror-stricken, he could only execute himself as gaily as he might: “But Lady Margaret, please make one small exception for me!” Of course she replied what was evident—that she did not call him a foreigner—but the slip betrayed a truth. Except for a moment’s personal introduction, he was a foreigner, and there was no reason why she should like him unless she were bored by natives.

Always conscious of this barrier, he hid among the herd of foreigners till he found his relations fixed. He never felt himself in society, and never knew definitely what was meant by those who were in it. He saw a score of societies quite independent of one another: the smallest and “smartest,” almost wholly strange to him; the sporting world; the legal, ecclesiastical, military, naval, City, artistic, county, Scotch—nebulous groups, as strange to each other as to him. After eight or ten seasons he professed to know less about society than when he made his first appearance. An American who neither hunted nor raced, neither shot nor fished nor gambled, and was not marriageable, had no need to think of society at large. Ninety-nine houses in a hundred were useless to him. Society had no unity; one wandered about in it like a maggot in cheese; it was not a hansom cab, to be got into, or out of, at dinner-time.

In seven years he could remember only two scenes that seemed to have any meaning for him, and he never knew what the meaning was. One was at Devonshire House, an unpremeditated reception. Mme. de Castiglione entered, the famous beauty of the Second Empire; the most refined society in the world instantly formed a lane and stood to stare, while those behind mounted on chairs; stared completely out of countenance, the lady fled the house at once. This was all! The other was at Stafford House, April 13, 1864, when, in a Paolo Veronese gallery, Garibaldi, in his gray capote over his red shirt, received all London, and three duchesses literally worshipped at his feet. What social, moral, or mental development these pointed out was beyond any process yet reached by the education of Henry Adams.

From the Court a private secretary got nothing. Royalty was in abeyance. The nicest distinction between the very best society and the second-best was their attitude towards royalty; the one regarded it as a bore, and avoided it. He never exchanged ten words with any royal person; he knew no one who would have given five shillings for a royal opinion on any subject. Rank had slight value compared with a good partner before midnight or a good supper after.

He grew to loathe the sight of his Court dress; to groan at every announcement of a ball; to dread every formal dinner. The greatest social event gave not half the pleasure that one could buy for ten shillings at the opera, and not a fourth of the education. Yet Lothrop Motley, among the very best judges, said to him that the London dinner and the English country house were the perfection of human society. Adams meditated. Motley could not have meant the cuisine, which was Gunter’s; nor the toilettes; nor the manners, notorious; nor the taste, worse. Perhaps he meant that in certain houses the tone was easy, the talk good, the standard of scholarship high. Even there the adjectives needed qualification. Within that relatively small, liberal, literary circle, the American Legation was at home; perfect only in the eyes of a Harvard College historian. They could teach little worth learning; their tastes were antiquated; their knowledge, ignorance to the next generation; fatal for future purposes, they were only English.

Yet the one thing needful for a private secretary was that he should actually be at home. He studied what seemed the favorite accomplishment of society. Perhaps his nervousness deceived him; but he conceived that the perfection of human society required that a man should enter a drawing-room where he was a total stranger, and place himself on the hearth-rug, his back to the fire, with an air of expectant benevolence, without curiosity, much as though he had dropped in at a charity concert, kindly disposed to applaud the performers and to overlook mistakes. This ideal rarely succeeded in youth, and towards thirty took a form of modified insolence; but about sixty it mellowed into deference to the young which had extraordinary charm. Unfortunately Adams could not wait till sixty; and the English air of patronage would earn no income anywhere else.

After five or six years one acquires the habit of going from one strange company to another without thinking much of one’s self or of them, as though silently reflecting that, “in a world where we are all insects, no insect is alien; perhaps they are human in parts”; but the dreamy habit of mind that comes from solitude in crowds is not fitness for success except in London. England’s social coinage had no currency elsewhere.

Englishwomen, from the educational point of view, could give nothing until they approached forty years old; then they became very interesting—to the man of fifty. The young American was not worth the young Englishwoman’s notice. His susceptible nature was left to the mercy of American girls, which was professional duty rather than education as long as diplomacy held its own.

Thus his third season saw the end of his diplomatic education, and began for him the social life of a young man more at home in England than anywhere else. Close relation in London is a personal mystery as profound as chemical affinity. Thousands pass, and one separates himself from the mass to attach himself to another, and so make, little by little, a group.

By such chances he breakfasted with Sir Henry Holland and there met a Cambridge undergraduate, Charles Milnes Gaskell. A visit to Cambridge followed; but what affected his whole life was the intimacy then begun with Milnes Gaskell and his circle, just about to enter the world. Intimates are predestined. He had jostled princes and loafers; visited every part of the United Kingdom; acquired habits of Sunday calls; escorted Americans to St. James’s; and all this gave him nothing to do, and was life wasted. On the other hand, his few personal intimacies concerned him alone; and chance made him almost a Yorkshireman.

More than any other county, Yorkshire retained a sort of social independence of London. The Yorkshire type had always been the strongest of the British strains; London could never quite absorb it, nor it love London. This must have been the reason why he was drawn there. Monckton Milnes might draw him, but James Milnes Gaskell held him: a man of the generation of 1830; a voracious reader and admirable critic; an adorer of Canning; rich by Yorkshire standards; indolently powerful; unwilling to move. To an American he was a character more unusual than his distant cousin Lord Houghton.

Mrs. Milnes Gaskell and her sister, Miss Charlotte Wynn, made the friendship a compliment as well as a pleasure. In England the family is a serious fact; once admitted to it, one is there for life. London might vanish, but Yorkshire lived for its friends.

In 1857 Mr. Milnes Gaskell bought Wenlock Abbey. The Prior’s house, a charming fifteenth-century specimen, had been left to decay as a farmhouse. She put it in order, and in the autumn of 1864 Adams was one of her first guests, driving about Wenlock Edge and the Wrekin, learning the loveliness of that exquisite country and its curious antiquity. It was a new and charming existence; ideal repose and rural Shakespearian peace—but a few years of it were likely to complete his education, and fit him to act a fairly useful part in life as an Englishman, an ecclesiastic, and a contemporary of Chaucer.

## Chapter 14

The campaign of 1864 and the reëlection of Mr. Lincoln set the American Minister on so firm a footing that he could safely regard his own anxieties as over, and the anxieties of Earl Russell and the Emperor Napoleon as begun. With a few months more, his own term would end, and he might look forward to return. His son no longer fretted; the time for going into the army had passed. If he were to be useful at all, it must be as a son, and as a son he was treated with indulgence and trust. He knew that he was doing himself no good by staying in London, but thus far he had done himself no good anywhere.

At this point, six months were dropped out of his London life. The climate told on some of the family; physicians prescribed a winter in Italy; the private secretary was detached as escort. He gained an education as Italian courier while the Civil War came to its end. The Cornice in vettura was delightful; Sorrento in winter offered hills and grottoes; Rome at Easter was an experience; the journey north through Perugia and Sienna a dream; the Splügen Pass worth seeing; Paris always to be seen; Baden, with fashionable Europe and America watching the Duke of Hamilton improve his social advantages by the conversation of Cora Pearl, added its touch.

The assassination of President Lincoln fell on the party at Rome, where it seemed singularly fitting to that nursery of murderers and murdered. Again one went to meditate on the steps of the Santa Maria in Ara Cœli; nothing happened. The travellers changed no plan; the Minister did not recall them. When the private secretary sat down again at his desk in Portland Place, he saw a world beyond connection with the past. His identity—if a bundle of disconnected memories be an identity—seemed to remain, but his life was broken into separate pieces; he was a spider, and had to spin a new web.

All his friends looked singularly commonplace without uniforms, and hastened to get married and retire into back streets and suburbs. The Minister was going home “next fall”; then “next spring”; then President Johnson quarrelled with the Senate, and things stayed unchanged. The routine of English society, after becoming a habit, threatened to become a vice. Had Adams shared a single taste with young Englishmen, he would have been lost; but his hack in Rotten Row was not a taste. Evidently he must set to work; he must get a new education; begin a career of his own.

Nothing was easier to say. Two careers were closed. For the law, diplomacy had unfitted him; for diplomacy, he already knew too much. Any one who had held, during the four most difficult years of American diplomacy, a position at the centre of action could not beg a second-rate post to bore himself doing nothing till the next President should turn him out. In any ordinary system he would have been called back to the State Department, but between President and Senate, service became a delusion. He saw no road; in fact there was none. His friends tried paths he could not take. One profession alone seemed possible—the press. The press was an inferior pulpit; an anonymous schoolmaster; a cheap boarding-school; but still the nearest approach to a career for the literary survivor of a wrecked education. For the press, then, he decided to fit himself; and since he could not go home to get practical training, he set to work to do what he could in London.

He drew breath only in the atmosphere of English methods and thoughts; he could breathe none other. England grew more agreeable and amusing. Lord Palmerston died; Lord Russell vanished; the conservatives came in; traditionally easier to deal with. Minister Adams’s personal weight increased year by year. The private secretary had only to reckon breakfasts, dinners, receptions, balls, theatres, country-parties; so many cards to be left; so many Americans to be escorted—the routine of every young American in a Legation; all counting for nothing in sum, leading nowhere except Portland Place and the grave.

The English habit of mind deepened its ruts every day. It was like the London drawing-room, a comfortable and easy spot, filled with bits and fragments of incoherent furnitures, never meant to go together, and arranged in any relation without making a whole, except by the square room. About innate tastes no one has the right to doubt; least of all the Englishman, for his tastes are his being; he drifts after them as a honey-bee drifts after his flowers, and in England every one must drift with him. Most drifted to the race-course or the moors; a few towards books or science; a number took to what, for want of a better name, they called Art.

The Minister had his æsthetic rag-bag: Wren’s city churches of a Sunday; coin sales at Sotheby’s. The son took alternate sales of drawings, engravings, water-colors. The difference between them was only a difference of direction. Of all supposed English tastes, that of art was the most alluring and treacherous. Once drawn into it, one had small chance of escape, for it had no centre or circumference, no beginning, middle, or end, and no conceivable result as education. William Hunt came, painted the Minister’s portrait, talked constantly, and went. Adams did not know enough to learn. He ran to Paris when he could, for sunshine; sought out a friend in the Rue du Bac; talked Beaux Arts; brought back less than he carried; English life made French art seem worst of all. England made bric-à-brac of all art.

In Yorkshire at Thornes, he met the man who drove him furthest in this English garden of innate disorder called taste: Francis Turner Palgrave—critic, anthologist, poet—clamorous, ferocious in judgment; and Thomas Woolner—sculptor, vehement; and Stopford Brooke—taste moderated by clerical propriety. Among these men, one wandered off into paths too devious for an American foot. He would have done better to go on the race-track, so far as concerned a career.

Fortunately he knew he knew nothing. He took Palgrave’s word about a Rafael, Woolner’s about a Turner; the dealers pooh-poohed them; then watched them at sales and bid over them. He once bought a water-color from the artist’s studio and had it doubted an hour afterwards where he took it to be framed. Internal evidence was against it. At a small auction he picked up for shillings a dirty red-chalk sketch like a figure in the Parnassus; one expert dismissed it; another appealed to water-marks; a scholar painfully deciphered a few lines of old verse scrawled on the back; a sculptor swore the museum was a fool. He kept the drawing on his mantelpiece forty years, and never cared whether it were Rafael’s or not. The experts had affirmed it to be worth a certain moiety of twelve shillings. His education had profited to that extent—his amusement more.

Art was a superb field for education, but always the same old signpost reappeared—battered and illegible. There was no next station. All the art of ten centuries had brought England to stuff which Palgrave and Woolner brayed in their mortars; derided, tore in tatters, howled at. What result could a student reach? Once, at dinner, Stopford Brooke abruptly asked him whether chaos were not better than death. Truly the question was worth discussion. For his part, neither chaos nor death helped a career. Both led him into an English dilettante museum of scraps, with nothing but a wall-paper to unite them. He went to sales and bought what he was told to buy—a classical drawing here; an unfinished Girtin or Cotman there, because more likely from nature. They made awkward spots on the wall as they did on the mind. The effect was spotty, fragmentary, feeble. The British mind was constructed in that way—boasted of it, and held it to be philosophy and method.

Turn from art to letters, and the same dangers appeared. The historical school was a playground of traps. One fell into antiquarianism. For one who nourished a weakness for what was called history, all British literature of the century was antiquarianism or anecdotage; no one except Buckle tried to link it with ideas, and Buckle was thought to have failed. Macaulay was the English historian. Adams admired him, but felt that any one who imitated him would perish. He was a dramatist; a painter; a poet, like Carlyle. This might be English genius; but the method that ended in Froude and Kinglake could hardly be sound for America where passion and poetry were eccentricities.

While he drifted, old American friends came abroad. Dr. Palfrey, busy with his History of New England, took the Puritan seriously and needed a scapegoat. The picturesque but unpuritanic Captain John Smith served. He suggested that Adams, who wanted a position, should throw a stone in the North American Review at Smith’s relations with Pocahontas. The task seemed amusing. Adams planted himself in the British Museum and patiently worked over all the material till he sent it to the editor. It appeared in January, 1867.

Surely, here was something to ponder—as a step in education! In spite of wishes and intentions; in spite of war and diplomacy; in spite of a determination to be actual and practical, Henry Adams found himself, at twenty‑eight, still in English society, dragged on one side into English dilettantism, which of all dilettantism he held the most futile; and, on the other, into American antiquarianism, which of all antiquarianism he held the most foolish. This was the result of five years in London. Even then he knew it to be a false start. If he were ever to amount to anything, he must begin a new education, in a new place, with a new purpose.
